title: The Iron Tithe
logline: Sent to retrieve a stolen relic before the midwinter rite, a mountain blacksmith's apprentice learns that bringing it home will cost her more than the village's paid protection.
premise: In a poor mountain village bound to an exploitative midwinter compact, a blacksmith's apprentice is sent to recover a relic stolen by raiders. The relic must be presented at the rite or the village loses the winter protection it has paid for in iron for three generations. She is very good at her craft and very bad at deciding what she owes people, and the recovery forces both capacities into the same decision. What she brings back is not what the village believes it is, and the person who made it is the master who raised her. Someone chooses, and pays.

audience.reader_promise: A finished moral choice, paid for, with the relic home or refused and the raising altered; no cheat, no sermon.

setting.period: Nameless secondary-world mountain winter; late-medieval tools, law, and travel
places: Kett, a poor mountain village and its forge
the high pass and the raider camp
the midwinter rite ground at the Toll ward-stone
rules_of_the_world: Magic exists only as already-bound institutional rites and objects; no character can cast, improvise, or personally wield it.
The winter ward over Kett is real. It is renewed only when the contracted token is presented at the midwinter rite. If it is not presented, the ward lapses over that valley.
The ward is fed by a yearly measure of worked iron, which the rite consumes. The labour is the price. The demanded measure has grown across three generations.
The Ward-nail in Kett's keeping is a forgery made by Harn forty years ago and has been accepted at every rite since.
Forty years ago, in a famine year, the Wardens took the original nail as surety for a short measure. Harn forged a replacement so the rite could proceed.
A competent smith can read maker, ore, and approximate age by eye, ring, and grain. This is craft, not magic, and it cannot be fooled by sentiment.
Winter travel is slow and dangerous. Distance and weather are binding. The midwinter date does not move.
Kett is poor. It cannot buy another compact, hire protection, or relocate before spring.
The Wardens are human, legal, and exploitative. They are neither demons nor fools, and they have a monopoly on a real ward.
Raiders are human and materially motivated. They are not an ancient evil and not the only opposition.
No prophecy, chosen lineage, or awakening power exists as a plot mechanism.
The original Ward-nail cannot reappear to resolve the plot. Magic cannot make the forgery true.

prose_touchstones: Ursula K. Le Guin, the workaday passages of the Earthsea stories
K.J. Parker, the unsentimental craft of metal
Kent Haruf, plain sentences and physical work
forbidden_tics: more than one figure of speech per paragraph
fate, prophecy, bloodline, or old-magic vocabulary
weather as mood without pressure on a body or a clock
two characters agreeing at length about an absent third
lyric catalogues that do not change a choice

action_adventure.evidence: Joss crosses winter passes and takes the relic back from raiders under time pressure.

coming_of_age.evidence: An apprentice chooses what she owes, leaving unexamined loyalty for a decided debt.

crime.evidence: A relic-theft and a forty-year forgery are crimes that shape both plots.

dark_fantasy.evidence: The ward consumes worked iron; protection is real and eats labour.

detective.evidence: Joss reads maker and age from slag and grain as if taking evidence.

drama.evidence: The story is the choice between debts; without that decision it is only a fetch.

family_drama.evidence: Master raised her; the forgery is a family secret that breaks or binds them.

fantasy.evidence: A real winter-ward, paid in iron, makes the relic's return a matter of survival.

gothic.evidence: A winter village keeps a forty-year secret in its holy iron.

low_fantasy.evidence: The compact is the spine; without the costly ward the deadline and price vanish.

mystery.evidence: Clues in the metalwork reveal the forgery and recontextualize the master's teaching.

mythic.evidence: A midwinter rite renews a compact; ritual is furniture, not fate.

political_thriller.evidence: The Wardens' growing tithe is institutional exploitation, not a conspiracy plot.

sword_and_sorcery.evidence: A personal retrieval from raiders; combat is brief and unromantic.

thriller.evidence: Midwinter is a lit fuse; recovery and exposure both threaten.

tragedy.evidence: Someone pays an irrevocable price; the brief forbids a tragic fall as the shape.

western.evidence: A hard landscape and a poor community facing raiders, used as colour.

arousal.evidence: Midwinter clock, the theft, the confrontation: regular pressure, not a crisis chain.

bittersweetness.evidence: Recovery and rupture arrive together; every gain spends a loyalty.

character_complexity.evidence: Joss and Harn have human motives, inner splits, and costs on both sides.

cliffhanger_frequency.evidence: Some scenes end on open stakes; most turn and resolve a local value.

conflict_density.evidence: The two plots tax each other; nearly every choice spends one to serve the other.

diversity_representation.evidence: A woman smith as lead; identities are not the subject.

emotional_depth.evidence: What she owes is examined until it changes what she does.

emotional_range.evidence: Duty, shame, anger, craft-pride, and grief share the eight scenes.

empathy_elicitation.evidence: Sympathy for Joss at work, then for Harn's old reason, then for both in the choice.

humor_presence.evidence: A dry remark at the anvil; humour never structures a scene.

moral_ambiguity.evidence: The forgery was mercy; the compact is legal theft; no clean virtue available.

mystery_complexity.evidence: Planted marks in the metal pay off when she reads the recovered nail.

narrative_complexity.evidence: Two plots, each with a because-link into the other, told linearly.

pacing_intensity.evidence: Eight scenes in seven thousand words; developments come steadily.

philosophical_depth.evidence: Debt, true work, and the ethics of a useful lie steer the climax.

relationship_centrality.evidence: Apprentice and master are the second plot and the brake on the first.

suspense_threat.evidence: Ward-lapse, exposure, and winter travel threaten throughout.

symbolism_allegory.evidence: True weight, the master's mark, and consumed iron carry the argument.

transformation_arc.evidence: She moves from owing everyone to choosing one debt and paying it.

valence.evidence: The ending grants no restoration; a necessary payment, not a ruin.

violence_level.evidence: A raid's damage and a struggle for the relic; impact shown, not dwelt on.

worldbuilding_detail.evidence: Forge practice, the tithe, and winter travel have consistent costs.

must_include: recovery of the Ward-nail before the midwinter rite
Joss discovers by craft that the nail is Harn's forgery
confrontation in which Harn's old reason is human and his current defence is not
choose-and-pay ending, visible on body, object, or rite
exploitative iron tithe to the Wardens
status quo at the forge before the journey
must_avoid: triumph or tragedy as the ending shape
reappearance of the original relic as a fix

keep_in_mind: PREMISE (exactly one): Keeping a useful lie for love leads to a debt the next generation pays. Prove this. Cut anything that does not.

CORE CONFLICT: Joss insisting on recovering and presenting the Ward-nail in time, versus the truth that the nail is Harn's forty-year forgery and that presenting it would make her the next keeper of a lie her craft cannot honestly pass. The Wardens' compact and the raiders are external pressure, not the core.

CRUCIBLE: Joss cannot walk away. Winter closes the roads; Kett loses the ward if the nail is not at the rite; Harn raised her in his house and his trade, and leaving him is leaving her only family and her living. Name this bond whenever a reader could ask why she does not simply leave.

Two plots only. External: recover the Ward-nail before midwinter. Relationship: Joss and Harn, and what the forgery does to the raising. Each must cost the other. At least one because-link in each direction.

Joss's ruling passion: to make true work and to discharge every visible debt. She is competent at the first and bad at ranking the second. Harn's ruling passion: no child of Kett dies for a missed tithe if a lie will prevent it.
Want versus need. Joss wants the nail home and Harn and Kett intact. She needs to choose a single debt and pay it. The climax forces the want and the need apart.
Growth axis: from owing-everyone (loyalty as paralysis) to choosing-one-debt and paying it in a visible act.
First appearance: sympathy through work, cold, and a debt she cannot refuse. She is struggling, not merely enduring. No wimp stretch.

Plant: in the opening, Joss rejects a piece as false-weight or wrong-handed. Payoff: she reads the recovered Ward-nail the same way. Harn's finishing habit is visible to a student, invisible to a worshipper.

The ending is a choice and a payment, visible on the body or the object or the rite. Not a triumph. Not a tragedy. No original relic. No magical fix. No death used as punctuation unless that death was already the named price.

Do not give Harn a villain's motive. Forty years ago the Wardens took the original as surety in a famine year; he forged a replacement so the rite could go on. The reason was mercy. It is not defensible now because the village has lived on a fraud, the penalty for exposure exceeds a missed year, and he let her love a man who was also a lie.

Antagonists are plural and human: raiders (hungry, perhaps from a settlement that already lost its compact), Harn (protecting the lie), the Wardens (a legal monopoly on a real ward, tithe grown across three generations). Never let the raiders carry the moral weight alone.
Magic is never a solution. No character casts, improvises, or wills power. The ward is real, institutional, and already priced.

Names for stability: Joss (apprentice, woman, twenty-three); Master Harn (sixty-three); village Kett; the Ward-nail; the Wardens of Toll. A reeve or rite-keeper may press the village debt. Do not add a romance.

Register: forge detail, weather, weight of things. If a camera cannot see it and a microphone cannot hear it, rewrite it. Subtext in the Harn/Joss scenes; they will not say what they mean when it costs them.
Equalise forces. Harn has trust, history, and the proven winters. Joss has craft-sight and, once recovered, the nail itself. The Wardens have the ward. Do not make anyone stupid to move the plot.
Status quo first: the forge, the tithe as ordinary burden, what the nail means, before the recovery journey begins in earnest.
Motif: true weight versus false; the ring of a weld; iron consumed and gone. Recur, do not lecture.
Carry exposition on conflict. Facts about the compact, the famine year, and the forgery arrive as weapons, boasts, slips, or accusations, never as briefings.
Scene default is pressure. Outcomes are no, yes-but, or no-and-worse. A clean yes ends tension and must be rare.
